 writing a simple for-loop to find the high tide
    Myfanwy Johnston <mrow...@gmail.com> Feb 14 08:58AM -0800  

    Hey y'all,
     
    I'm trying to write a for-loop that finds the high tide in a vector of
    10-minute tide recordings. When it finds the high tide, I'd like it to
    spit that value into a new vector. I generated some simple sample data
    (attached) that simulates the dataset with integers. So far, I have:
     
    d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)
     
    m=0
     
    for (i in 1:length(d$numbers)) {
     
    if(d$numbers[i]>=m) {d$numbers[i] -> m}
     
    else {m=m}
     
    }
     
    This successfully spits out the first "high tide" value (8), but I don't
    know how to make it keep going through the whole vector to get the next two
    values (which should be 5 and 8, respectively).
     
    Any help would be greatly appreciated!
     
    Best,
    Myfanwy
     
    --
    Myfanwy Johnston
    University of California at Davis
    Biotelemetry Lab
    +1.530.205.5243

     

    Anna Steel <annae...@gmail.com> Feb 14 09:25AM -0800  

    Hi Myfanwy,
     
    This is a slightly different logical approach, but it will create a vector
    of c( 8, 5, 8) as you suggest:
     
    d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)
     
    highs = NA
    j=1
    for (i in 2:(length(d$numbers)-1))
    {
    if(d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i-1] & d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i+1])
    {highs[j] <- d$numbers[i] ; j = j+1}
    }
     
     
     
     
    However, I wonder if you also don't want a way to extract the row in which
    the high tides occur? Here is the same code with a few extra lines to pull
    that information as well and put it all into one dataframe:
     
    d <- read.csv("numbers.csv", header=T)
     
    highs = data.frame(tide.height = rep(NA,10), tide.row = rep(NA,10))
    j=1
    for (i in 2:(length(d$numbers)-1))
    {
    if(d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i-1] & d$numbers[i]>=d$numbers[i+1])
    { highs$tide.height[j] <- d$numbers[i]
    highs$tide.row[j] <- as.numeric(rownames(d)[i])
    j = j+1}
    }
    highs = highs[!is.na(highs$tide.height),]
     
     
    The 'rep(NA,10)' at the top and the matching line at the bottom to remove
    extra NAs is a bit messy, plus the value of 10 would potentially have to be
    increased for larger datasets. If anyone has better code to clean that up,
    please do!
     
     
    - Anna

    Noam Ross <noam...@gmail.com> Feb 14 09:26AM -0800  

    Myfanwy,
     
    pastecs::turnpoints does exactly this:
     
    library(pastecs)
    data = read.csv("numbers.csv")
    turn = turnpoints(data$numbers)
    hightides = data$numbers[turn$peaks]
    hightides
     
    [1] 8 5 8
     
    The object turn$peaks is a logical vectors with TRUE in any position which
    is a peak in your vector. turn also has turn$pits and a lot of other
    diagnostic data.
     
    Another solution, suggested by Ben Bolker on StackOverflow
    here<http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6836409/finding-local-maxima-and-minima>is
     
    turn2 = which(diff(sign(diff(data$numbers)))==-2)+1
    data$numbers[turn$peaks]
     
    diff-sign-siff here gets the differences between each consecutive number,
    and checks when these differences change sign from positive to negative (1
    to -1 as returned by sign). If you change the -2 to 2, you'll get the pits
    instead of the peaks. The +1 at the end deals with the fact that
    diffreturns a result ` shorter than the original.
     
    If your data are noisy Tim Poisot has a solution here:
    http://rtricks.wordpress.com/2009/05/03/an-algorithm-to-find-local-extrema-in-a-vector/,
    and the discussion to StackOverflow above has some discussion of options.
     
    Noam

Tim Poisot posted a function for finding peaks in noisy data here: http://rtricks.wordpress.com/2009/05/03/an-algorithm-to-find-local-extrema-in-a-vector/. findpeaks takes a bandwidth (bw=) argument, which is the width of a sliding window in which peaks are calculated. If you set the window to half the period of the tides, you’ll only get one peak per tide. I’ve pasted the function and an example below.

findpeaks <- function(vec,bw=1,x.coo=c(1:length(vec)))
{
  pos.x.max <- NULL
    pos.y.max <- NULL
    pos.x.min <- NULL
    pos.y.min <- NULL

  for(i in 1:(length(vec)-1))     { 
    if((i+1+bw)>length(vec)) {
        sup.stop <-  length(vec)}else{sup.stop <- i+1+bw
                }
        if((i-bw)<1){inf.stop <- 1}else{inf.stop <- i-bw}
        subset.sup <- vec[(i+1):sup.stop]
        subset.inf <- vec[inf.stop:(i-1)]

        is.max   <- sum(subset.inf > vec[i]) == 0
        is.nomin <- sum(subset.sup > vec[i]) == 0

        no.max   <- sum(subset.inf > vec[i]) == length(subset.inf)
        no.nomin <- sum(subset.sup > vec[i]) == length(subset.sup)

        if(is.max & is.nomin){
            pos.x.max <- c(pos.x.max,x.coo[i])
            pos.y.max <- c(pos.y.max,vec[i])
        }
        if(no.max & no.nomin){
            pos.x.min <- c(pos.x.min,x.coo[i])
            pos.y.min <- c(pos.y.min,vec[i])
        }
    }
    return(list(pos.x.max,pos.y.max,pos.x.min,pos.y.min))
}

Example:

x <- sin((1:200)*pi/50) + 2 + rnorm(200, 0, 0.1) # generate some noisy periodic data

fp = findpeaks(x, bw=10) #only count peaks that are the max over a period of 10 points

plot(x, type="l")
points(fp[[1]], fp[[2]], lwd=2, col="red")

Note that fp[[1]] and fp[[2]] are the x and y values at the peaks. fp[[3]] and fp[[4]] are the same for the pits.

Thanks Noam, that function worked beautifully to find the peaks.  It gets a little trickier for the minimums in the data attached, though - when I ran it, fp[2] had about 43250 values, while fp[4] had only 51 values.  Since there are two high tides and two low tides in semidiurnal tidal zones (a high high tide, a low high tide, a high low tide, and a low low tide), it looks like the function is treating about half the high low tides as high tides.  Natural data is so messy :)  No need to keep working on this (the assignment has passed), but if you're curious, here's my code:

d <- read.csv("fielddata.csv", header=T)
fp <- findpeaks(d$Level, bw=30)
plot(d$Level, type="l", ylab="Water Level (ft)")
points(fp[[1]], fp[[2]], col="red")
points(fp[[3]], fp[[4]], col="dodgerblue")

length(unlist(fp[2]))
length(unlist(fp[4]))

Thanks so much for everyone's time on this - I've learned a lot!

Best,
Myfanwy

Note that fp[[1]] and fp[[2]] are the x and y values at the peaks. fp[[3]] and fp[[4]] are the same for the pits.

    Myfanwy,
     
    pastecs::turnpoints does exactly this:
     
    library(pastecs)
    data = read.csv("numbers.csv")
    turn = turnpoints(data$numbers)
    hightides = data$numbers[turn$peaks]
    hightides
     
    [1] 8 5 8
     
    The object turn$peaks is a logical vectors with TRUE in any position which
    is a peak in your vector. turn also has turn$pits and a lot of other
    diagnostic data.
     
    Another solution, suggested by Ben Bolker on StackOverflow
    here<http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6836409/finding-local-maxima-and-minima>is
     
    turn2 = which(diff(sign(diff(data$numbers)))==-2)+1
    data$numbers[turn$peaks]
     
    diff-sign-siff here gets the differences between each consecutive number,
    and checks when these differences change sign from positive to negative (1
    to -1 as returned by sign). If you change the -2 to 2, you'll get the pits
    instead of the peaks. The +1 at the end deals with the fact that
    diffreturns a result ` shorter than the original.
     
    If your data are noisy Tim Poisot has a solution here:
    http://rtricks.wordpress.com/2009/05/03/an-algorithm-to-find-local-extrema-in-a-vector/,
    and the discussion to StackOverflow above has some discussion of options.
     
    Noam

    turnpoints is robust to repeated maxima, but the diff-sign-diff solution is
    not. With repeats at the peaks, turnpoints$peaks will return TRUE values at
    the FIRST of the repeated peak values. diff-sign-diff will miss it
    altogether.
